clinicalPearls: Gingivitis is reversible inflammation confined to the gingiva without loss of periodontal attachment or bone
The cardinal sign is bleeding on gentle probing or brushing, alongside redness, swelling, and loss of the normal stippled contour
It is overwhelmingly plaque-induced, so improved oral hygiene and professional cleaning usually reverse it within days to weeks
Hormonal changes in pregnancy and puberty, and certain medications, can exaggerate the gingival response to plaque
Unlike periodontitis, probing depths remain shallow and there is no true pocketing or attachment loss
Untreated gingivitis is a risk state that may progress to periodontitis in susceptible individuals
Necrotising gingivitis is a distinct painful form with ulcerated, punched-out interdental papillae and characteristic malodour
Persistent gingival inflammation despite good hygiene should prompt consideration of systemic or drug-related causes
reference.pathophysiology: Plaque-induced gingivitis develops when microbial biofilm accumulates at the gingival margin and triggers a localised host inflammatory response. Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability cause the classic erythema, oedema, and bleeding tendency, while the junctional epithelium remains intact and attachment is preserved, making the condition reversible. If the biofilm persists, the chronic inflammatory infiltrate can, in susceptible hosts and under modifying influences such as hormonal changes, systemic disease, or medications, evolve toward the attachment and bone loss that define periodontitis.
additionalDifferentials: Gingival manifestations of leukaemia or other systemic illness
additionalInvestigations: Assessment of bleeding on probing and plaque indices
Periodontal probing to confirm absence of attachment loss
Review of medications and hormonal or systemic factors
Radiographs when needed to exclude bone loss
Blood investigations if systemic disease is suspected
redFlags: Spontaneous gingival bleeding or florid enlargement suggesting leukaemia or a bleeding disorder
Painful necrotising gingivitis, particularly in immunocompromised patients
Gingival changes that fail to resolve with good hygiene, indicating an underlying systemic cause
reference.prognosis: Plaque-induced gingivitis is fully reversible with effective plaque control, but if neglected it can act as a precursor to irreversible periodontitis in susceptible people.
pitfalls: Assuming all gingival inflammation is simple plaque-induced gingivitis and missing early periodontitis
Overlooking systemic, hormonal, or drug-related contributors to gingival changes
Attributing spontaneous bleeding to local causes when a haematological disorder is present
Failing to reinforce oral hygiene, leading to recurrence
management: Mechanical biofilm removal is the mainstay, with professional scaling and supragingival debridement to disrupt plaque at the gingival margin
Reinforce daily plaque control through effective toothbrushing and interdental cleaning, which usually reverses the inflammation within days to weeks
Short-term adjunctive antiseptic mouthrinse such as chlorhexidine where mechanical control is temporarily inadequate
Identify and modify aggravating factors, reviewing implicated medications and managing hormonal or systemic contributors such as pregnancy or diabetes
Structured dental recall with reassessment of bleeding on probing and plaque indices to confirm resolution
Refer to a dental hygienist or periodontist and escalate to periodontal probing if attachment loss or true pocketing emerges, signalling progression to periodontitis
